You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test case org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtilsEqualsIndexOfTest.testContainsNone_CharArrayWithSupplementaryChars involves characters U+20000 and U+20001, which are Unicode supplementary characters represented by surrogate pairs in Java ("\uD840\uDC00" and "\uD840\uDC01").

The current bug report states that StringUtils methods do not handle Unicode 2.0+ supplementary characters correctly. Specifically, the containsAny/containsNone methods do not handle such supplementary characters properly.

The code snippet for StringUtils.containsNone(CharSequence, char[]) iterates over the CharSequence character by character with cs.charAt(i) (line 1680), which retrieves a single char (16-bit) rather than a complete supplementary code point (which requires decoding surrogate pairs). Similarly, the search characters are of type char array and the code checks for single char matches (line 1682). This means the method will compare only BMP characters properly, but supplementary characters that consist of surrogate pairs will cause incorrect behavior since each surrogate half will be treated as an independent char.

The comment on line 1683 states "missing low surrogate, fine, like String.indexOf(String)", showing that the method does not currently account for low surrogates or surrogate pairs.

Because the test passes supplementary character strings (e.g., CharU20001.toCharArray()) to the method, the containsNone method incorrectly checks each surrogate individually rather than the full supplementary character, leading to wrongful positive or negative matches.

Hence the bug arises because containsNone does not account for surrogate pairs or supplementary code points, resulting in incorrect detection of Unicode supplementary characters in input CharSequences and search char arrays.

Recent bug reports are mostly unrelated, discussing indexOf or javadoc issues and do not mention supplementary character handling.

Therefore, the root cause is clear: containsNone and possibly other related methods do not process supplementary Unicode characters correctly because they iterate and compare at the char level, ignoring surrogate pairs.

The fix involves changing the iteration logic to handle supplementary characters properly, likely by operating on code points rather than chars.

This diagnosis matches the current bug report and explains the test failure.
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test failure arises because StringUtils.containsNone(CharSequence, char[]) does not handle Unicode supplementary characters correctly. The method iterates over the input CharSequence character by character using cs.charAt(i), which returns a single 16-bit char. However, Unicode supplementary characters (above U+FFFF), such as U+20000 and U+20001 used in the test, are encoded in Java as surrogate pairs (two chars). The method compares each char individually against the char array searchChars, so it compares surrogate halves separately, not as full code points. This leads to incorrect detection of supplementary characters, causing the method to fail for strings containing such characters. The comment in the code indicates this limitation: "missing low surrogate, fine, like String.indexOf(String)". The root cause is that the method does not account for surrogate pairs or process code points correctly, leading to erroneous matches or misses for Unicode 2.0+ supplementary characters. Recent bug reports do not address this issue and thus are not relevant. The fix requires modifying containsNone to iterate and compare characters as code points rather than individual chars.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
